detailed_description: The Line Chart Generator is a web-based data visualization tool that enables developers to create multi-series line charts using client-side JavaScript rendering. This tool leverages the D3.js library to generate responsive SVG graphics with Cartesian coordinate systems, supporting both linear and logarithmic scales. Users can analyze temporal data patterns, compare multiple datasets through dual-axis configurations, and apply cubic spline interpolation for smoothed trend visualization. The generator supports JSON and CSV data inputs with automatic type inference for numerical/time-series values. Developers can customize tick formatting, axis labels, and color palettes using Hex/RGB values while maintaining accessibility standards through ARIA-compliant SVG attributes. The tool's backend-agnostic design allows data processing entirely in-browser, ensuring privacy for sensitive datasets. Technical features include WebXR compatibility for immersive visualizations and support for Canvas 2D rendering fallbacks. Exported charts maintain vector precision through SVG paths and PNG rasterization at 400dpi, suitable for documentation and presentations.
usage_steps: 1. Access the tool's data editor to paste CSV/JSON content or manually input values in the tabular interface.
2. Use the 'Series Mapping' panel to assign columns to X/Y axes and select interpolation method (linear/cubic/step).
3. Configure dual Y-axes by toggling 'Secondary Axis' for comparative datasets with differing magnitude ranges.
4. Adjust time scale settings via the 'Axis Format' menu to parse dates in ISO/D3 format for temporal visualizations.
5. Apply custom color gradients using the Hex input fields or select from Material Design swatches in the 'Theme Editor'.
6. Export charts via the 'Download' button, choosing between SVG (with embedded CSS) or PNG formats at custom resolutions.
usage_examples: Financial analysts tracking monthly stock price volatility across multiple companies with volume comparisons.
Biologists visualizing bacterial growth curves under different temperature conditions over 72-hour periods.
Web developers comparing HTTP/2 versus HTTP/3 request latency across global CDN nodes.
Meteorologists displaying temperature anomalies against 30-year averages with confidence interval shading.
